title: Die Wassernixe
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 79. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved (daß, mußte, wußte, Müh).
about: KHM 79, one paragraph long and one of the barest tales in the collection: two children fall into a well, are set to impossible work by the nixie who lives at the bottom, and slip away one Sunday while she is at church. The flight that follows belongs to a very old and very widespread pattern — the obstacle-flight, in which each thing thrown behind the fugitive becomes a mountain — and Grimm gives it stripped to the bone: no names, no rescue, no reward, only three mountains and a nixie trudging back down her own well.

sentences.t: Ein Brüderchen und ein Schwesterchen spielten an einem Brunnen, und wie sie so spielten, plumpten sie beide hinein.
sentences.l: A little brother and a little sister were playing by a well, and as they played so, they both plumped in.
sentences.i: A little brother and a little sister were playing by a well, and as they played they both tumbled in.
sentences.n: plumpen is the sound of the fall itself, close to English “plop”. Brüderchen and Schwesterchen are diminutives; the children are given no names at all, here or anywhere in the tale.

sentences.t: Da war unten eine Wassernixe, die sprach „jetzt hab ich euch, jetzt sollt ihr mir brav arbeiten,“ und führte sie mit sich fort.
sentences.l: Down below there was a water-nixie; she spoke “now I have you, now you shall work hard for me,” and led them away with her.
sentences.i: Down at the bottom there was a water nixie, who said: “Now I have you — now you shall work hard for me,” and she led them away with her.
sentences.n: A Wassernixe is a female water-spirit of well and pond, not of the sea. brav here means “properly, with a will”, not “brave” — a false friend worth remembering. “mir arbeiten” puts her in the dative: work for her.

sentences.t: Dem Mädchen gab sie verwirrten garstigen Flachs zu spinnen, und es mußte Wasser in ein hohles Faß schleppen, der Junge aber sollte einen Baum mit einer stumpfen Axt hauen; und nichts zu essen bekamen sie als steinharte Klöße.
sentences.l: To the girl she gave tangled, nasty flax to spin, and it had to haul water into a hollow cask; the boy, however, was to hew a tree with a blunt axe; and nothing to eat did they get but stone-hard dumplings.
sentences.i: To the girl she gave tangled, filthy flax to spin, and she had to carry water into a hollow cask; the boy was to fell a tree with a blunt axe; and they got nothing to eat but dumplings as hard as stones.
sentences.n: hohl is simply “hollow”, and the tale does not say more; the cask is understood not to hold what is poured into it, so the work can never be finished. These are the classic impossible tasks of the world below. The girl is das Mädchen, grammatically neuter, so German says “es mußte”, “it had to”. “nichts bekamen sie als…” — als here is “except”.

sentences.t: Da wurden zuletzt die Kinder so ungeduldig, daß sie warteten, bis eines Sonntags die Nixe in der Kirche war, da entflohen sie.
sentences.l: Then at last the children grew so impatient that they waited until one Sunday the nixie was in church, and then they fled.
sentences.n: “so ungeduldig, daß sie warteten” — impatient, and so they waited: the German lets the oddity stand. Their patience is at an end, and what they wait for is the one hour the nixie is sure to be away.

sentences.t: Und als die Kirche vorbei war, sah die Nixe daß die Vögel ausgeflogen waren, und setzte ihnen mit großen Sprüngen nach.
sentences.l: And when the church was over, the nixie saw that the birds had flown out, and set after them with great bounds.
sentences.i: And when church was over, the nixie saw that the birds had flown, and came after them in great bounds.
sentences.n: The children are called birds only here, in the nixie’s own way of seeing it; ausfliegen is what fledglings do when they leave the nest. That a water-spirit spends her Sunday morning in church is one of the pleasant oddities of these tales, and Grimm neither explains it nor apologises for it.

sentences.t: Die Kinder erblickten sie aber von weitem, und das Mädchen warf eine Bürste hinter sich, das gab einen großen Bürstenberg, mit tausend und tausend Stacheln, über den die Nixe mit großer Müh klettern mußte; endlich aber kam sie doch hinüber.
sentences.l: But the children caught sight of her from afar, and the girl threw a brush behind her; that gave a great brush-mountain with a thousand and a thousand spikes, over which the nixie had to climb with great trouble; at last, though, she did get across.
sentences.i: But the children caught sight of her from far off, and the girl threw a brush behind her, and it made a great mountain of bristles with a thousand and a thousand spikes, over which the nixie had to climb with great labour — yet at last she got across.
sentences.n: The obstacle-flight begins: brush, comb, mirror, each becoming the mountain its own surface suggests. “das gab” = that made, that produced, as one says of a recipe. Müh = modern Mühe, trouble, effort.

sentences.t: Wie das die Kinder sahen, warf der Knabe einen Kamm hinter sich, das gab einen großen Kammberg mit tausendmal tausend Zinken, aber die Nixe wußte sich daran fest zu halten und kam zuletzt doch drüber.
sentences.l: When the children saw that, the boy threw a comb behind him; that gave a great comb-mountain with a thousand times a thousand teeth, but the nixie knew how to hold fast to it and got over it at last after all.
sentences.i: When the children saw that, the boy threw a comb behind him, and it made a great mountain of comb-teeth, a thousand times a thousand of them; but the nixie knew how to hold fast to it, and got over in the end after all.
sentences.n: The count rises from “tausend und tausend” to “tausendmal tausend” — the tale escalates by arithmetic. Zinken are the teeth of a comb or the prongs of a fork.

sentences.t: Da warf das Mädchen einen Spiegel hinterwärts, welches einen Spiegelberg gab, der war so glatt, so glatt, daß sie unmöglich drüber konnte.
sentences.l: Then the girl threw a mirror backwards, which gave a mirror-mountain; it was so smooth, so smooth, that she could not possibly get over it.
sentences.i: Then the girl threw a mirror behind her, and it made a mountain of mirror, so smooth, so smooth, that she could not possibly get over.
sentences.n: hinterwärts (backwards) in place of the “hinter sich” of the first two throws: the third time round, the tale varies its own formula. “daß sie unmöglich drüber konnte” leaves the verb of motion out — “could not possibly [get] over”.

sentences.t: Da dachte sie „ich will geschwind nach Haus gehen und meine Axt holen und den Spiegelberg entzwei hauen.“
sentences.l: Then she thought “I will go home quickly and fetch my axe and hew the mirror-mountain in two.”
sentences.i: Then she thought: “I will go home quickly and fetch my axe and split the mirror-mountain in two.”
sentences.n: entzwei = in two, apart. The only axe this tale has named is the blunt one she set the boy to work with; whether it is meant to be the same axe is left open.

sentences.t: Bis sie aber wieder kam, und das Glas aufgehauen hatte, waren die Kinder längst weit entflohen, und die Wassernixe mußte sich wieder in ihren Brunnen trollen.
sentences.l: But by the time she came back and had hewn the glass open, the children had long since fled far away, and the water-nixie had to trundle herself back into her well.
sentences.i: But by the time she came back and had hacked through the glass, the children had long since escaped far away, and the water nixie had to take herself off back into her well.
sentences.n: “sich trollen” = to take oneself off, to slink away — a dismissive, faintly comic word, and the last thing the tale grants the nixie. The children are never heard of again.
